How to Find Free Parcel Data for Any US County

A practical guide to finding and downloading free parcel boundary data for US counties. Learn which agencies publish parcel GIS data, the common formats, and how to download it without a paid data subscription.

Muhammad Junaid BaigOctober 6, 20268 min read

Parcel data — the legal boundaries of land ownership — is one of the most requested GIS datasets in the world. It powers property tax systems, urban planning, real estate analysis, environmental research, and much more.

The good news: in the United States, parcel data is almost always public. The bad news: it is scattered across thousands of county and municipal GIS portals, each with its own format, licensing terms, and download process. This guide shows you how to find it efficiently.

Who publishes parcel data?

Parcel data is almost always maintained at the county level. In most states, the county assessor or the county GIS department is the authoritative source.

  • County assessor offices — maintain ownership and valuation records
  • County GIS departments — publish the spatial parcel layer
  • State-level GIS clearinghouses — aggregate county data into statewide layers
  • Regional councils of governments (COGs) — sometimes host regional compilations
  • Private aggregators (Regrid, CoreLogic, LightBox) — paid, but useful for gaps
Rule of thumb
Always start with the county. Statewide compilations often lag behind the county by months or years.

Step 1: Identify the county GIS portal

The fastest way to find a county's GIS portal is a simple Google search:

[county name] [state] GIS portal
or
[county name] parcel viewer
or
[county name] open data

Common portal URLs look like:

  • gis.[countyname].gov
  • maps.[countyname].gov
  • [countyname].maps.arcgis.com
  • data.[countyname].gov

Step 2: Look for these common delivery methods

Counties publish parcel data in one of a few standard ways. Recognizing them will save you time.

1. ArcGIS REST FeatureServer (the best case)

If the county runs ArcGIS Online, you will see a URL that looks like:

https://services.arcgis.com/.../Parcels/FeatureServer/0

This is the easiest to work with. You can paste it directly into Geo Server Data Downloader and export the whole dataset as Shapefile, GeoPackage, or GeoJSON in a few minutes.

2. Pre-packaged downloads (ZIP files)

Many smaller counties publish a "Download Parcels" button that delivers a ZIP containing a Shapefile. These are usually updated monthly or quarterly. Look for links named "GIS Data Download" or "Data Downloads" on the county GIS page.

3. Interactive parcel viewers

Some counties only offer a web-based viewer. Check whether the viewer is powered by ArcGIS, QGIS Server, or a custom stack — if it is ArcGIS, there is almost certainly a FeatureServer URL behind the scenes that you can find by looking at the network tab in your browser's developer tools.

4. Statewide clearinghouses

If the county does not publish its own data, check your state's GIS clearinghouse. Good examples:

  • California: CAGIS / California State Geoportal
  • Texas: TNRIS / Texas Geographic Information Office
  • New York: NYS GIS Clearinghouse
  • Florida: FGDL (Florida Geographic Data Library)
  • Washington: WAGDA / Washington State Geospatial Open Data Portal

Step 3: Verify license and attribution requirements

Parcel data is public, but "public" does not always mean "do whatever you want with it." Common license types you will encounter:

  • Public domain — no restrictions
  • Creative Commons (CC0, CC-BY, CC-BY-SA) — requires attribution, sometimes share-alike
  • Custom government license — check for restrictions on commercial use
  • Paid commercial license — some counties restrict redistribution
Attribution is not optional
If the license requires attribution, include the county name and data year in your project. Losing track of this can cause serious legal problems down the road.

Common fields you will see in parcel data

Most county parcel datasets contain a fairly consistent set of attributes:

FieldMeaning
APN / PINAssessor's Parcel Number — the unique ID for the parcel
OWNER_NAMEOwner of record (may be an individual, trust, or corporation)
SITUS_ADDRPhysical property address
MAIL_ADDROwner mailing address (often out of state)
LAND_USEClassification code (residential, commercial, industrial, etc.)
ACRESCalculated lot size in acres
ASSESSED_VALUEValue used for property tax purposes
YEAR_BUILTYear the primary structure was constructed
SALE_PRICEMost recent sale price
SALE_DATEDate of most recent sale

Step 4: Download and convert

If the county publishes a FeatureServer URL, download the data through Geo Server Data Downloader:

  1. Copy the FeatureServer URL for the parcels layer.
  2. Open the Downloader page.
  3. Paste the URL and click Add Layer.
  4. Choose your export format in the Bulk Export dialog (GeoPackage is best for large parcel datasets).
  5. Download the ZIP archive.

Frequently asked questions

Is parcel data free in every state?

In almost every US state, parcel data is legally public. However, some counties charge a nominal fee for bulk data extracts, and a few states restrict commercial redistribution. Always check the county's terms of use.

Why is my parcel dataset missing some parcels?

Common reasons: the county only publishes parcels within its jurisdiction, some parcels are unclassified or "in transition" during reassessment, or the dataset simply has not been updated since the last property transfer.

How often is parcel data updated?

Highly variable. Large, tech-savvy counties update daily. Small rural counties may update once a year. Check the metadata on the county's GIS portal — it usually lists a "last updated" date.

Summary

Parcel data is out there and it is free — the challenge is finding it. Start with the county, identify whether they publish an ArcGIS FeatureServer, download the data through a browser-based tool, and always check the license before using it in a project.
